title: Count a text file
text:
To count nonempty lines in a small file:
1. Open the file.
2. Trim each line.
3. Increment a counter only if the result is nonempty.
Blank lines do not contribute to the count.

title: Map example

title: Canal path diary
text: For twelve mornings I walked the canal path before work. On the first morning I counted nine bicycles and three walkers. On the second morning rain kept nearly everyone away. I wrote the weather beside each count because a quiet path during a storm should not be compared directly with a sunny day. The third morning brought a maintenance van, so I paused my count rather than treating a blocked path as an ordinary sample. Several neighbours suggested turning the counts into an argument for wider paths. I would like wider paths too, but this notebook cannot establish demand across the whole town. It covers one stretch at one hour, and it says nothing about afternoons or weekends. My strongest conclusion is modest: keeping consistent notes helped me notice how much the weather and maintenance changed the scene. I plan to repeat the exercise in spring with the same route and starting time.

title: Drying clay
text: Our pottery group tried three drying schedules on equal-sized clay tiles. The first group dried uncovered, the second under loose fabric, and the third inside an open-sided box. We weighed each tile every morning for eight days and wrote down visible cracks. The uncovered tiles lost weight fastest and showed the most early cracks. The boxed tiles dried slowly; two still felt damp on day eight. The fabric group sat between the other two. We did not control room humidity, and the tiles came from only one batch of clay. That means the observations are useful for planning another workshop trial, rather than proving one schedule is best for all pottery. Next time we will record humidity and use more than one clay batch. Nobody fired these tiles, so this trial does not report fired strength.
